content: Prosthetics and orthotics professionals who are unable to leave their jobs for full-time training can benefit from interdisciplinary teaching and learning approaches. These approaches integrate prosthetics, orthotics, therapy, and medicine into shared training sessions, fostering teamwork among graduate health and rehabilitation professionals. This is particularly crucial during practical clinical training, where students focus on assessment, prescription, and treatment evaluation. Such sessions can also be applied to common theoretical subjects. Professional standards for prosthetists, orthotists, associates, and technicians are well-established and maintained by national professional bodies and the International Society for Prosthetics and Orthotics (ISPO). These standards serve as benchmarks for policymakers, government ministries, regulatory bodies, and funding agencies, guiding education and curriculum development. The World Health Organization (WHO), in collaboration with ISPO, has developed detailed education and training guidelines for prosthetics and orthotics professions, which are widely accepted by governments and non-governmental organizations. ISPO provides information packages to support the establishment or restructuring of prosthetics and orthotics training courses. These packages outline learning objectives, syllabi, and arrangements for final examinations. They also include guidelines for program evaluation and international recognition of training programs. Training content should align with international and national educational standards, including those set by ISPO. Theoretical training typically covers clinical subjects such as anatomy, physiology, prosthetics and orthotics science, pathology, and orthopedics, as well as technical topics like mechanics, biomechanics, materials science, and technology. Practical training emphasizes the application of theoretical knowledge to skills in designing, producing, adapting, and aligning prostheses and orthoses, ensuring functionality, comfort, and safety for users. Quality considerations must be prioritized. Students in prosthetics and orthotics programs should develop problem-solving skills and adopt reflective practices, learning from daily and case-by-case experiences. Continuous learning should be viewed as an integral part of their professional lives. Professional communication skills are also essential. Courses should provide foundational knowledge on user-centered care, disability issues, multidisciplinary teamwork, professional codes of conduct and ethics, management tools, work safety, referral processes, national healthcare systems, and the provision of other mobility assistive products. Additionally, students should gain exposure to clinical research, technical innovations, and community development related to prosthetics and orthotics. All professionals working with users must adhere to a professional code of conduct and ethics. For example, the Health and Care Professions Council in the United Kingdom outlines 15 standards of proficiency for prosthetists and orthotists, including practicing safely, maintaining fitness to practice, working autonomously, respecting diversity, maintaining confidentiality, and ensuring quality in practice. Student selection for prosthetics and orthotics training should be transparent and based on academic criteria. Candidates should possess the necessary educational qualifications to fully assimilate course content and demonstrate aptitude for clinical and technical work. They should also exhibit values and attitudes conducive to working with individuals with disabilities. Efforts should be made to ensure gender balance among trainees, as this can improve access to services for women. Special initiatives may be required to encourage women to pursue training and employment in this field. Additionally, student intake should reflect cultural, ethnic, and demographic diversity, and candidates from underserved areas should be prioritized to address workforce needs in remote and rural locations. Graduates of prosthetics and orthotics programs typically receive certification upon completing their training. However, they often lack experience, which they gain through reflective practice and continuing professional development (CPD) throughout their careers. Graduates should complete internships or supervised clinical practice before obtaining national accreditation and certification to practice independently. Early-career professionals usually provide a defined range of treatments under the supervision of senior colleagues, who may require additional training to fulfill mentoring roles. In countries without local prosthetics and orthotics education programs, training professionals abroad can be a viable solution. However, this requires significant financial investment, and trainees must be carefully selected to ensure long-term benefits. Graduates returning from international training programs should have access to employment opportunities and support from experienced colleagues. International training institutions should ensure that their curricula are relevant to the local contexts in which graduates will work. Prosthetics and orthotics professionals should collaborate with medical faculties and educational institutions to ensure appropriate course content. They may also prepare targeted training modules and participate as lecturers. Health, allied health, and social care professionals working with prosthetics and orthotics service units require additional training, ranging from basic sensitization to specialized knowledge. This can be achieved through courses, seminars, and experiential learning, such as multidisciplinary teamwork. Service providers should ensure that all personnel have access to CPD opportunities to maintain and enhance their competencies. CPD improves service quality, effectiveness, and efficiency while incorporating new clinical and technical developments. CPD pathways may include formal training, such as short courses for career progression, and informal learning, such as reflective practice, team discussions, evidence-based practice, and participation in seminars and workshops. Access to scientific literature and training in research appraisal are essential for fostering continuous knowledge growth among clinicians.
